ambiguities.description: The text requires receipt by the "date, time, and location indicated above", but no physical or electronic submission location (address, portal, email) is given in this chunk, so the bidder cannot tell where to deliver the proposal.

The RFP says the preferred Vendor shall have experience implementing solutions for cities of similar size and scope, but neither 'similar size' nor 'scope of services' is defined, so a bidder cannot tell whether its references qualify; the bidder would ask what population, budget or module scope counts as similar.

Best-of-breed HCM vendors are invited to respond, but it is unclear whether such a response is evaluated as a standalone award or only alongside an ERP vendor's proposal, which affects teaming and pricing strategy; the bidder would ask how best-of-breed submissions are evaluated.

The text requires the solution to include the modules and functionality in the Requirements document but does not state whether those requirements are mandatory pass/fail or scored, nor whether deviations may be proposed; a bidder would ask how compliance is evaluated and whether alternative functionality is acceptable.

The implementation approach is left open (phased or vendor-recommended with City approval) with no stated timeline, milestones or go-live date, so a bidder cannot size the schedule or price phasing; the bidder would ask whether a target implementation timeline or phasing structure is prescribed.

The City reserves the right to modify or reschedule the timeline, so bidders cannot rely on the stated dates; a bidder would ask whether the Proposals Due date and the March 2025 implementation start are firm or subject to change.

The Go Live date of January 1, 2027 is stated as an evaluation criterion rather than a contractual milestone, and it is unclear whether it is a hard requirement for the proposed timeline or merely a scored factor. The bidder would ask whether a proposal with a later Go Live date would be rejected or only scored lower.
The demo script is described as pre-defined but is not included in this text; bidders would ask where the script is provided and whether it is issued with the RFP or later.
The pre-demo meeting is mentioned without a date, time or format, so bidders cannot plan attendance; they would ask when and how it is held.
The proposal deadline is deferred to Section 3, which is not in this chunk; the bidder needs the exact closing date and time (and time zone) to schedule submission.

The required order of proposal contents is defined in a table that is not included in this chunk, so the bidder cannot yet structure the PDF; the bidder would ask for that table or the required section order.

The required proposal sections are referred to as "outlined below" but the list is not contained in this text, so the bidder cannot tell what sections and order are required to avoid being deemed non-responsive; the bidder would ask for the complete list of required proposal sections and their order.

The pricing section requires one sheet per deployment option "if applicable (SaaS or on-premises)", but it is unclear whether a bidder must price both deployment options or only the one it proposes; the bidder would ask whether both SaaS and on-premises pricing sheets are required.

The 100-word limit is stated for "each response" in the Requirements document, but it is unclear whether it also applies to the narrative sections (Implementation, Support) or only to the per-requirement comments; the bidder would ask which responses the limit covers.

The text requires references 'similar in size and scope to the City's project' but does not define the City's size or scope here; a bidder would ask what thresholds (e.g., population, budget, module count) make a reference comparable.
The security administration item lists 'SSO, SAML, etic', where 'etic' appears to be a typo or truncation; a bidder would ask what additional capabilities are intended.

The text says comments "should include a brief explanation" while also stating vendors "must" provide a rating and comment for every item; it is unclear whether the brief explanation is mandatory or only preferred, and what level of detail counts as brief.

The text states the document is not a comprehensive list of all the City's requirements but that it will be incorporated into the signed contract; a bidder would ask whether requirements not listed in the document are also contractually binding.

The sample row shows "(limit to 100 words)" inside the response cell while the instruction says to limit each line-item response to 100 words; it is unclear whether the 100-word limit applies to the whole line item (rating plus comment) or only the comment text.
The deadline for written questions is not stated here; it is only referenced as a date in Section 3 – Timeline, so a bidder cannot tell from this text when the question cut-off falls.

The text requires immediate written notice of errors but does not define what "immediately" means or whether notice after the question deadline but before proposal submission still preserves the proposer's rights.

The submission deadline is not stated here but is referenced to Section 3 – Timeline and the "project schedule", while Section 6 refers to "the date indicated in the project schedule"; a bidder would ask which document controls and confirm the exact date and time for electronic submission.

The text does not say how or where electronic proposals are to be submitted (portal, email address, format), only that Section 5 – Vendor Instructions governs; a bidder would ask for the submission channel and any file-size or format limits.

The insurance clause requires a certification of insurance and an underwriter's endorsement but states no coverage types, limits or additional insured parties, so the bidder cannot price insurance or confirm compliance; the bidder would ask what coverages, limits and additional insured wording are required.

The template requires a separate pricing sheet per deployment option, but this chunk does not identify which deployment options must be priced; the bidder would ask which options (e.g., SaaS vs. on-premise) must each receive a sheet.

The template lists "Project and Grant Accounting" twice under Financial Modules, so it is unclear whether two separate line items are expected or this is a duplication; the bidder would ask how to price it.

The exhibit does not state whether the three references must be live on the same ERP product/modules being proposed, or whether any current customer of the bidder qualifies; the bidder would ask what qualifies a customer as "current" and whether product/scope match is required.
The exhibit does not say whether the reference contacts may be contacted by the issuer or whether prior consent must be obtained, which affects how references are selected and cleared.

The table does not state how many prior customer references are required or whether the two slots are a minimum or a maximum; a bidder would ask whether exactly two references are required or whether additional references may be submitted.

The fields "Population" and "Number of Employees" are undefined as to whether they refer to the reference customer's organisation or to the population served by the software; a bidder would ask which figure is expected.

client_situation.text: The RFP is issued by the City of Federal Way, Washington, a city incorporated in February 1990 that changed from a council-manager to a mayor-council form of government in November 2010.

The City is residential and commercial, with an estimated 22,485 people employed within the city limits, and its comprehensive plan calls for a vibrant City Center with mixed-use development and public transportation access.

The City currently runs a legacy environment that it intends to replace with an integrated ERP solution; the RFP presents tables describing the current environment and which solutions are in scope, but the chunk text does not name the specific systems.
The business driver is process improvement: the City expects to improve processes through the new systems and to adopt the best practices offered by the selected Vendor.
The City wants a Vendor with experience successfully implementing the proposed solutions for cities of similar size and scope of services.
The City is also open to best-of-breed Human Capital Management Vendors, provided their solution can integrate with the selected ERP system.
The City's user base for pricing purposes is 130 named and 85 concurrent Financials users, and 400 FTEs plus 744 W2s for Human Capital Management.

goal.text: The City intends to purchase an integrated ERP solution covering the modules and functionality defined in the Requirements document provided with the RFP.

The required Financial modules are General Ledger, Budget, Project and Grant Accounting, Purchasing and Contract Management, Accounts Payable, Accounts Receivable, Capital Assets and Enterprise Cashiering.
The required Human Capital Management modules are Human Resources, Time and Attendance and Payroll.
The City expects implementation using a phased approach, or another approach recommended by the selected Vendor and approved by the City.
Implementation is scheduled to run from March 2025 through January 2027, following contract negotiations in January 2025 and later.
The proposal must deliver a cover letter executive summary (two pages maximum), a completed Requirements document, Exhibit A pricing, an implementation plan and a support plan.

Pricing must cover software Year 1, implementation services (implementation, data conversion, training, report development, integration, travel, other) and subscription or maintenance for Years 2 through 10.

success_criteria.text: Proposals are scored by an evaluation committee on Software (30 points), Implementation (25 points), Technology (15 points), Vendor (15 points) and Cost Value (15 points).
The Implementation criterion requires Go Live for all modules in scope by January 1, 2027.

Finalists must present functional and technical product demos to the City following a pre-defined Demo Script, and demo evaluation covers adherence to that script and demonstrated ability to meet the City's functional and technical requirements.
Vendor questions are due August 28, 2024 at 3:00 p.m. PT, and the City posts all questions and answers on its website by September 5, 2024.
Proposals are due September 17, 2024 at 3:00 p.m. PT by email to Thuch.Mam@FederalWayWA.gov, and late submissions will not be considered.
Software missing a significant number of required features and technology preferences may be eliminated from consideration.

Every requirement line item must carry a rating (4 = standard and available, 3 = third-party integrated, 2 = modification with estimated cost, 0 = not available, F = future release with month and year) plus a comment of no more than 100 words, and blank responses may cause the proposal to be rejected as incomplete.
The City may award on the basis of the initial proposal alone, without discussions, and no contract is awarded until approved by City Council.

constraints.text: The proposal must be one electronic PDF of no more than 100 pages (sample contracts excluded) plus one completed Requirements document in MS Word format, with no marketing literature.

The Requirements document is provided as a separate Word document that must be submitted without any change to format, font, numbering or page breaks, with no hyperlinks and no cross-references to other line items.

Pricing must be submitted on the Exhibit A Pricing Summary template, be comprehensive including all taxes and available discounts, and remain valid for 180 days from the response date, with a separate sheet per deployment option (SaaS or on-premises).

The technology overview must cover hosted, on-premises and SaaS architecture options, deployment options, data center locations and redundancy, hardware specifications, mobile hardware and OS options, remote access, integration tools and methodologies, and software update scheduling.

The security overview must cover the security model and standards, security administration including SSO and SAML, multi-factor authentication, and security breach customer communication, response and cost.

References must be submitted on Exhibit B forms with three current and two prior customers of similar size and scope, with preference for Washington State public sector clients, and any contract terminated for convenience or non-performance or legal action with a customer in the past five years must be disclosed.

Sample contract documents must be provided (Statement of Work, Perpetual Software License or SaaS License Agreement, Maintenance or Support Agreements, Service Level Agreements), and any exceptions to the RFP must be documented.
All data, materials and documentation originated and prepared for the City become the City's property, and no Vendor may mark its entire submittal proprietary.

solution.summary: The bid proposes a single integrated ERP suite for the City of Federal Way — Financials (General Ledger, Budget, Project and Grant Accounting, Purchasing and Contract Management, Accounts Payable, Accounts Receivable, Capital Assets, Enterprise Cashiering) plus Human Capital Management (Human Resources, Time and Attendance, Payroll) — delivered as a configured, hosted-or-on-premises commercial product with implementation services, not a custom build. Delivery runs in phases from March 2025 to a full-suite Go Live before January 1, 2027: mobilise and process design, then Financials, then HCM and integrations, then stabilisation and post-go-live support. The team is a named vendor implementation group (project manager, functional leads per module, data conversion and integration specialists, report developers, trainers and change managers) working alongside City subject-matter experts whose time commitments are stated by role. Pricing is submitted on Exhibit A with a separate sheet per deployment option, itemised by module, service line and Years 2–10 subscription, and held firm for 180 days. A governance and compliance component carries the contractual, insurance, ownership and disclosure obligations — including the bid-phase question deadline — so they are not lost among the technical work.

components.title: Programme governance, contract and compliance obligations
components.description: A dedicated contract and compliance workstream runs from bid submission to close-out. It records the City's terms and conditions as accepted in full by submission of the proposal (R010), and confirms that no terms other than the City's are referenced in the response, so the proposal is not rejected as non-responsive (R110). It maintains a written RFP-error and clarification log: ambiguities, conflicts and omissions are notified to the City in writing as soon as identified, and the bidder accepts that failing to notify a known or reasonably knowable error before submission means it bids at its own risk with no later claim for compensation or time (R103). It tracks every addendum and confirms each is incorporated into the submitted proposal. It confirms that all data, materials and documentation originated and prepared for the City become City property (R025), that no part of the submittal is designated proprietary in its entirety and that the City alone determines what is proprietary under public disclosure law (R108), and that proposal development costs are borne by the bidder and not charged to the City (R105). Insurance is handled here: a certificate of insurance is provided before any work commences (R111), with an underwriter's endorsement carrying additional-insured wording and a surety admitted in the State of Washington (R112). The workstream also owns the monthly steering report to the City covering schedule, budget, risks and decisions.

claims.text: The City is the City of Federal Way, Washington, and the RFP requires insurance documentation naming it as an additional insured.

components.title: Bid-phase clarification and question management
components.description: A bid-phase workstream owns the City's question process end to end. All questions arising from the RFP, its exhibits and the separate Requirements document are consolidated, reviewed for commercial sensitivity and submitted in writing to the City before the August 28, 2024 3:00 p.m. PT cut-off, so the bidder meets the question deadline rather than losing the right to raise scope, pricing or contractual points (R004). The same log records the City's posted answers and any addenda issued by September 5, 2024, and each answer is traced into the Requirements document ratings, the Exhibit A assumptions and the implementation plan before submission, so the priced proposal reflects the City's clarifications rather than the bidder's reading of the original text. Questions that would reveal pricing strategy are phrased neutrally, and the log is retained as the audit trail for any later dispute about what the City confirmed.

claims.text: Vendor questions are due August 28, 2024 at 3:00 p.m. PT, and the City posts all questions and answers on its website by September 5, 2024.

components.title: Solution scope confirmation and Requirements document response
components.description: Before pricing is fixed, the team completes the City's ERP Requirements document in the supplied MS Word file and returns it as Section 2 of the proposal, with every line item rated on the City's scale (4 standard and available, 3 third-party integrated, 2 modification, 0 not available, F future release) and a comment of no more than 100 words explaining how the item is supported (R005, R011, R017). Where an item is rated 2, the estimated cost of the modification is stated against that line (R093). The completed document demonstrates that all Financial and HCM modules the City requires are offered by the proposed suite, which is what the Software criterion scores (R017). The same scope baseline drives the module-by-module configuration plan and the demo script mapping, so what is promised in the Requirements document is what is shown in the demo and built in implementation.

claims.text: The City's required Financial modules are General Ledger, Budget, Project and Grant Accounting, Purchasing and Contract Management, Accounts Payable, Accounts Receivable, Capital Assets and Enterprise Cashiering, and its required HCM modules are Human Resources, Time and Attendance and Payroll.

components.title: Phased implementation programme and project plan
components.description: The implementation is delivered in phases over the March 2025 to January 2027 window, sequenced so that all modules in scope are live before January 1, 2027 (R016, R018). Phase 1 mobilises the programme, confirms the process-improvement baseline and completes fit-gap against the City's best-practice expectations; Phase 2 configures and tests Financials; Phase 3 configures HCM and the integrations between them; Phase 4 runs integrated and parallel testing, cutover and go-live; Phase 5 stabilises and hands over to support. The approach is the phased approach the City contemplates, with any deviation recommended by the vendor submitted for City approval before it is adopted (R012). The proposal includes a sample project plan with phases, tasks, durations and dependencies, and states City resources by role, responsibility and average hours per month and vendor resources on the same basis, so the City can see the demand on its own staff (R012).

claims.text: Implementation is scheduled to run from March 2025 through January 2027, following contract negotiations in January 2025.
Go Live for all modules in scope by January 1, 2027 is an explicit evaluation criterion under the Implementation scoring category.

components.title: Process improvement, change management and training
components.description: Because the City's stated driver is process improvement rather than like-for-like replacement, the programme carries a process-improvement workstream that maps current City processes to the suite's standard best practices, quantifies the change for each affected process and agrees the target design with process owners before configuration. A structured change-management methodology and toolset — stakeholder analysis, impact assessment per role, communications plan, readiness assessments and a champion network — is applied across the 130 named and 85 concurrent Financials users and the HCM population (R012). Training is delivered by role and by module using a train-the-trainer model plus quick-reference materials, with competency checks before go-live and refresher sessions after it. Both workstreams are resourced in the plan and priced in the implementation services line.

claims.text: The City's user base for pricing is 130 named and 85 concurrent Financials users, and 400 FTEs plus 744 W2s for Human Capital Management.

components.title: Data conversion, integration and report development
components.description: A conversion workstream extracts, cleanses, maps, validates and loads legacy master and transactional data module by module, with a documented conversion methodology stating for each module the years of history, data elements and cleansing rules, and with at least two mock conversions and reconciliation sign-off by the City before cutover. Integration covers the interfaces between the Financials and HCM modules and to the City's remaining systems, using the suite's published integration tools and methodologies, and — where a best-of-breed HCM product is proposed instead of the suite's own HCM — a demonstrated, tested integration path to the selected ERP so the City's integration requirement is met (R007). Report development replaces the City's current reporting with a defined report inventory built in the suite's reporting tools, tested against legacy output. All three workstreams are itemised and priced separately in the implementation services section of Exhibit A.

claims.text: The City currently runs a legacy environment it intends to replace with an integrated ERP solution.

components.title: Demonstrations and evaluation support
components.description: For finalist stage the team prepares and delivers functional and technical demonstrations that follow the City's pre-defined Demo Script exactly, with a rehearsed script-to-screen mapping so every scripted scenario is shown in the sequence the City expects (R020). Each demo scenario is drawn from the City's own requirements and configured in a demonstration environment populated with City-like data, so the demo evidences the product's ability to meet the City's functional and technical requirements rather than a generic sales walkthrough (R021). The team also stands ready to supply additional information, interviews, follow-up demonstrations or written clarifications at the City's request, and to discuss best practices and user-preference configuration when invited (R022). Demo preparation is a scheduled task in the project plan with named presenters per module.

claims.text: Finalists must present functional and technical demos to the City following a pre-defined Demo Script, and demo evaluation covers adherence to that script.

components.title: Exhibit A pricing and commercial model
components.description: Pricing is submitted on the City's Exhibit A Pricing Summary template as Section 3 of the response, with a separate sheet for each deployment option offered so the City can compare SaaS and on-premises on a like-for-like basis (R044, R047). Year 1 software is itemised by module with stated assumptions, covering the eight Financial modules priced for 130 named and 85 concurrent users and the three HCM modules priced for 400 FTEs and 744 W2s (R115, R116, R117). Implementation services are itemised across Implementation, Data Conversion, Training, Report Development, Integration, Travel and Other, each with stated assumptions and each sufficient to reach go-live (R048, R118). Subscription or maintenance is itemised for each of Years 2 through 10 with stated assumptions (R049, R119). All figures are comprehensive, including all applicable taxes and every available discount, and the pricing is held valid for 180 days from the response date (R045, R046).

claims.text: Pricing must cover software Year 1, implementation services and subscription or maintenance for Years 2 through 10.

components.title: Hosted or on-premises deployment, technology and security architecture
components.description: The solution is offered as a commercial ERP product deployed either in the vendor's hosted/SaaS environment or on City infrastructure, with the proposal describing both architecture options, the deployment options and the data centre locations and redundancy model for the hosted option, plus hardware specifications for the on-premises option. Mobile hardware and operating system options, remote access capabilities and supported technologies, and the integration tools and methodologies are documented, as is the software update regime — whether updates are scheduled or automatic and on what cadence. Security is documented as a model and a set of standards: the security model, the standards the system meets, security administration including SSO and SAML, multi-factor authentication support, and the breach-handling process covering customer communication, response and cost. The same content forms the technical section of the demo and the basis of the Technology score.

claims.text: The City requires the technology overview to cover hosted, on-premises and SaaS options, data centre locations and redundancy, hardware, mobile, remote access, integration and update scheduling.

components.title: Support, service levels and post-go-live services
components.description: A support plan is submitted with the proposal covering support hours, guaranteed response times by severity, the resources available and the escalation path, with baseline and premium support levels compared side by side so the City can choose. Post-go-live tools and services — monitoring, release management, user administration and periodic health checks — are described, together with the backup strategy and the disaster recovery service covering backup, redundancy and location, again distinguishing baseline from premium. User groups and conferences available to City staff are listed as part of the ongoing capability-building offer. Support is priced within the Years 2–10 subscription line so the City sees the full ten-year cost.

claims.text: The City requires subscription or maintenance pricing for Years 2 through 10.

assumptions.text: The Requirements document supplied separately with the RFP is assumed to define the functional scope summarised in the RFP's module list, and the bid prices and configures to that document as issued rather than to any additional functionality.
The bid prices both a SaaS/hosted and an on-premises deployment option, each on its own Exhibit A sheet, so the City can compare them rather than assuming only the proposed option is required.
The January 1, 2027 Go Live is treated as a firm commitment in the proposed schedule, not merely a scored preference, and the plan is built backwards from it.
The March 2025 start and the stated proposal dates are assumed to hold as published, with any City rescheduling handled through a change order rather than absorbed in the fixed price.

The bid is submitted as a single integrated ERP suite covering both Financials and HCM, with best-of-breed HCM offered only as an alternative that carries a demonstrated integration to the ERP, since the RFP does not say how a standalone HCM submission would be evaluated.

Insurance is priced on the assumption of commercial general liability, professional liability, cyber liability and workers' compensation coverages with the City named as additional insured, since the RFP states no coverage types or limits.

The 100-word limit is applied to every per-requirement comment in the Requirements document and, for safety, to narrative responses as well, since the RFP does not say which responses the limit covers.

References are drawn from three current and two prior customers running the same product and modules, with Washington State public-sector clients preferred, and each reference is contacted for consent before submission.
The demo script is assumed to be issued to finalists with the notification e-mail, and demo preparation is scoped and priced as a fixed effort in the implementation services line.

The current environment tables are assumed to describe a set of legacy systems whose data is converted module by module with a stated history depth agreed during fit-gap, since the specific systems and data volumes are not given.

The August 28, 2024 question cut-off is assumed to be the only channel through which the City will answer scope and pricing questions, so all clarifications the bid relies on are submitted in writing before that date rather than raised later in the process.

risks.title: Requirements document not in hand, so scope and price rest on an unseen document
risks.description: The functional scope the bid must price and configure is defined in a separate ERP Requirements document that is not part of the RFP text available to the team. If the document contains line items beyond the module list summarised in the RFP, the bid either under-prices the work or must rate items it has not costed, and the Software criterion (30 points) is scored directly on that document. The bidder carries the cost of any rework to the Requirements ratings and Exhibit A after the document is received.
risks.justification: The scope baseline for both the Requirements response and the Exhibit A price is a document the team does not yet hold, and the RFP makes blank or unrated lines grounds for rejection as incomplete.
risks.mitigation: Obtain the Requirements document and Exhibit A before any pricing work starts; state in the proposal that the price is based on that document as issued and that line items not in it are out of scope and handled by change order.

risks.title: Go Live date treated as firm when the RFP only scores it
risks.description: The proposed plan commits to all modules live before January 1, 2027 and builds the schedule backwards from that date, but the RFP states the date as an evaluation criterion rather than a contractual milestone. If the City later treats it as a hard date, or if fit-gap reveals more configuration than expected, the bidder absorbs the cost of acceleration or carries the risk of a missed date on a fixed price. Conversely, if the City would have accepted a later date, the bid may have priced unnecessary contingency.
risks.justification: The RFP does not settle whether a later Go Live is rejected or merely scored lower, and the solution has chosen to treat the date as binding without a stated assumption to that effect in the commercial terms.
risks.mitigation: Ask the City in writing before August 28, 2024 whether a later Go Live is disqualifying or only scored lower, and state in the proposal that the January 1, 2027 date assumes timely City decisions, SME availability and no scope growth beyond the Requirements document.

risks.title: Proposal format and section order not fully specified, risking non-responsiveness
risks.description: The RFP refers to a required order of proposal contents and a list of required sections that are not present in the text available to the team, and it warns that deviations may be classified as non-responsive. The solution plans a 100-page PDF plus a Word Requirements document but cannot confirm the section sequence. A mis-ordered or over-length submission could be disqualified before it is scored.
risks.justification: The consequence of a non-responsive finding is total loss of the bid, but the solution's structure follows the RFP's stated components and the risk turns on a table the team has not yet seen.
risks.mitigation: Obtain the submission table and required section list from the City, build the PDF to that exact order, and run a page-count and format check against the 100-page limit before the September 17, 2024 deadline.

risks.title: Timeline can be rescheduled by the City after the price is fixed
risks.description: The RFP reserves the City's right to modify or reschedule the timeline, while the proposed solution assumes the March 2025 start and published dates hold and that any rescheduling is handled by change order. If the City moves the start or stretches the phases, vendor resources committed for the original window may not be available and the fixed price may no longer cover the delivery. The bidder either absorbs the difference or disputes it after award.
risks.justification: The RFP explicitly reserves the right to reschedule, and the solution's assumption that rescheduling is a change order is the bidder's reading, not something the RFP confirms.
risks.mitigation: State in the proposal that pricing is based on a March 2025 start and the published phase durations, and that a start delayed beyond an agreed threshold triggers a schedule and price adjustment.

risks.title: Both deployment options priced without knowing which are required
risks.description: The solution prices a SaaS/hosted option and an on-premises option on separate Exhibit A sheets, but the RFP does not say whether both must be priced or only the proposed one. Pricing both doubles the commercial and technical effort and risks the City comparing the two in a way that disadvantages the bid, while pricing only one risks a non-responsive submission. The bidder also carries the cost of documenting two architectures, two security models and two sets of hardware specifications.
risks.justification: The RFP's pricing template says one sheet per deployment option 'if applicable' without defining applicability, and the solution has resolved the ambiguity by pricing both.
risks.mitigation: Ask the City before the question deadline whether both SaaS and on-premises sheets are required, and if unanswered, submit both with a clear statement of which option the bidder recommends and why.

risks.title: Insurance priced without stated coverage types or limits
risks.description: The RFP requires a certificate of insurance and an underwriter's endorsement naming the City as additional insured but states no coverage types, limits or additional insured parties. The solution assumes commercial general liability, professional liability, cyber liability and workers' compensation. If the City's contract requires higher limits or coverages the bidder does not carry, the bidder faces unplanned premium cost or an inability to commence work, which delays the March 2025 start.
risks.justification: The RFP leaves the coverage schedule open, and the solution's assumption of four coverage lines is an inference rather than a confirmed requirement.
risks.mitigation: Ask the City for the required coverage types, limits and additional insured wording before submission, and confirm with the broker that the assumed coverages can be endorsed with a Washington-admitted surety before any work commences.

risks.title: Best-of-breed HCM evaluation path unclear, affecting teaming and price
risks.description: The RFP invites best-of-breed HCM vendors but does not say whether such a submission is evaluated standalone or only alongside an ERP vendor. The solution offers a single integrated suite with best-of-breed HCM only as an alternative carrying a demonstrated integration. If the City expected a standalone HCM award or a partnered submission, the bid may be scored against a structure it did not address, and the integration effort priced for the alternative may be misjudged.
risks.justification: The RFP does not settle how best-of-breed submissions are evaluated, and the solution has chosen a suite-first structure without confirming that choice with the City.
risks.mitigation: Ask the City how best-of-breed HCM submissions are evaluated and whether a partnered ERP-plus-HCM response is acceptable, and state in the proposal which structure is being submitted and on what basis it is priced.

risks.title: Demo script not issued, so demo preparation is scoped blind
risks.description: Finalists must demonstrate against a pre-defined Demo Script that is issued only with the finalist notification, yet the solution prices demo preparation as a fixed effort in the implementation services line. If the script covers scenarios outside the configured demonstration environment or requires modules not yet configured, the team must build additional demo content at short notice. The demo is scored on adherence to the script, so a poor fit costs evaluation points as well as effort.
risks.justification: The script is a referenced document not included in the RFP, and the solution's fixed demo effort is an assumption about its size and content.
risks.mitigation: State in the proposal that demo preparation is priced on a script of comparable scope to the requirements set, and reserve the right to re-scope demo effort once the script is issued; keep a rehearsed generic scenario library ready.

risks.title: Legacy systems and data volumes unknown, so conversion is under-scoped
risks.description: The RFP's tables describing the current environment and the systems in scope are not available, and the solution assumes a set of legacy systems converted module by module with history depth agreed during fit-gap. If the legacy estate is larger, dirtier or more numerous than assumed, data conversion and reconciliation effort grows after the fixed price is set. Conversion is a separately itemised and priced line, so the overrun lands directly on the bidder.
risks.justification: The specific systems and data volumes are not given in the RFP, and the solution's conversion scope rests on an assumption rather than on the City's inventory.
risks.mitigation: Ask the City for the current environment tables and data volumes before submission, and state in the proposal the assumed number of source systems, history years and cleansing rules, with additional conversions priced as change orders.

risks.title: Unreadable page may hide submission or pricing instructions
risks.description: Page 5 of the RFP is dominated by an image block that could not be read, and it may carry instructions on submission, pricing or scope that the bid does not reflect. If it contains a mandatory instruction, the proposal could be judged non-responsive or priced on a wrong basis. The bidder would only discover this after the deadline.
risks.justification: A page covering 42% of its area with an unparsed image is a real blind spot, and the RFP's submission and pricing rules are strict enough that a missed instruction is costly.
risks.mitigation: Obtain a readable copy of page 5 from the City or the issuing contact before the question deadline and confirm in writing that no instruction on that page has been missed.

risks.title: 100-word limit applied broadly may crowd out required narrative
risks.description: The solution applies the 100-word limit to every per-requirement comment and, for safety, to narrative responses as well, because the RFP does not say which responses the limit covers. If the limit does not apply to the Implementation and Support narratives, the bid may under-describe methodology, resourcing and support levels that carry 25 and 15 scoring points respectively. If it does apply and the bid ignores it, the submission risks being marked non-compliant.
risks.justification: The RFP's wording is genuinely unclear on the scope of the limit, and the solution has chosen the conservative reading, which trades evaluation strength for compliance safety.
risks.mitigation: Ask the City whether the 100-word limit applies to narrative sections, and if unanswered, keep per-requirement comments within the limit while writing full narrative sections and noting the interpretation in the cover letter.

risks.title: Reference qualification criteria undefined, risking a weak Vendor score
risks.description: The RFP requires three current and two prior customer references of similar size and scope, with preference for Washington State public sector clients, but does not define 'similar size', 'current' or whether references must run the same product and modules. The solution assumes references from customers running the same product and modules with Washington public-sector clients preferred. If the City applies a stricter test, the bid may lose Vendor points or be found non-responsive on references.
risks.justification: References carry 15 Vendor points and the criteria are undefined, but the solution's reference selection already targets the preferred profile, so the exposure is to scoring rather than to delivery.
risks.mitigation: Ask the City what qualifies a reference as similar in size and scope and whether product and module match is required, and obtain each reference's consent to be contacted before submission.
